blocks.text: Intro

A wheezy accordion plays a brief, waltz-like three-note pickup, recalling an earlier act. Detuned upright piano interrupts with a jaunty 4/4 shuffle at 94 BPM. Upright bass enters slightly late. Brushes and tin percussion settle into a crooked, comfortable groove. Muted trumpet offers two cheeky notes. Small, intimate room.
Verse 1

The same gravelly, whiskey-worn carnival barker from the opening number. Warm, practiced swagger, conversational spoken-sung patter. He’s entertaining the last few people in the tent. Affectionate, amused, completely at ease. Piano leaves generous space for his timing.

Last call. One more before you go.
We’ll keep it nice and quick.
A coin, a cup, a borrowed coat—
an old and serviceable trick.

Now watch the coin. No, watch the cup.
Yes, that one. Very good.
And if you’ve seen it all before,
act surprised, if you would.
Refrain

Melody opens naturally from the patter. Catchy, small-band swing, almost cheerful. Bass walks confidently; brushed snare keeps a light bounce. Trumpet gives a short, mischievous reply between phrases. No dramatic lift.

Watch where I point,
never where I stand.
The trick was never in the box, my friends,
the trick was always in the hand.
Verse 2

Back to easy patter. A little self-satisfied, as if sharing trade secrets. Piano answers with clipped chords. Accordion wheezes occasionally in the gaps. Scrap-metal percussion adds tiny, irregular accents. Nothing grows darker.

I hung a mirror by the door.
You’d stop to pick a fight
with someone who looked just like you,
and keep it up all night.

We’d roll the crates behind your backs,
we’d lock the loading gate.
The scale out back won’t weigh a soul—
it only weighs the freight.
Refrain
Exactly the same melody and volume. Slightly looser delivery, almost tossed away. The barker sounds pleased with himself. Trumpet heckles again; piano briefly gets ahead of the bass.

Watch where I point,
never where I stand.
The trick was never in the box, my friends,
the trick was always in the hand.
Bridge

The singer notices something across the room. His patter catches, but THE BAND DOES NOT STOP. Piano maintains its jaunty vamp. Bass and brushes keep walking. No ominous chord, no dramatic silence. Vocal becomes distracted, mildly incredulous, almost embarrassed.

Wait. That’s my jacket.
That’s my mark beside the door.
He’s working through my old routine—
a little faster than before.
He watches, momentarily forgetting he’s performing. Delivery becomes slower and more conversational, almost talking to himself. The band remains cheerfully indifferent.

I showed him where the hinge was.
I taught him sleight of hand.
Then he said, “Now watch the coin.”
I did. Well, I’ll be damned.
Short instrumental turnaround
Piano repeats its familiar figure. Muted trumpet returns with a casual two-note flourish. No musical acknowledgment of the revelation.
Final Refrain
Same familiar melody, smaller and more absentminded. No whisper, no sorrowful strain. The barker is watching somebody else’s act now. A trace of amusement remains.

Watch where he points,
never where he stands.
The trick was never in the box, my friends,
the trick was always in the hand.
Outro
Bass and piano carry the same easy shuffle. Vocal returns to intimate, offhand patter. He’s no longer addressing an audience so much as admitting something to himself. No emotional crescendo.

I built the box. I sold the smoke.
They said, “Enjoy the show.”
I almost told you how it worked.
But I stayed for one more go.
Instrumental ending

The singer falls silent. The band plays two more bars at exactly the same tempo. Accordion exhales a faint, familiar waltz-like phrase beneath the piano. Everyone lands on a slightly imperfect, ordinary final chord. Natural room decay. No dramatic sting, no fade.

notebook.style: Crooked vaudeville shuffle, 94 BPM, easy swing, disreputable bounce. The returning carnival barker from the opening number: gravelly, whiskey-worn male baritone, warm and mischievous, effortlessly charming, conversational spoken-sung patter slipping into natural melody. Same seasoned showman’s swagger, now performing for a nearly empty tent. Never sinister or melodramatic. Detuned upright piano drives a jaunty repeating vamp; upright bass walks slightly behind; brushed snare, tin taps and scrap-metal clinks make a loose junkyard rhythm. Muted trumpet heckles the singer with short comic replies; occasional wheezy accordion recalls the larger cabaret ensemble. Catchy, almost cheerful refrain, unchanged melody. At the bridge, his confidence briefly falters, but the band plays on, oblivious. No dramatic silence, swelling strings or grand revelation. Dry live-room acoustics, analog grit, imperfect timing. Final refrain stays small. Voice stops; band finishes two bars later.
notebook.idea: At the bridge, his confidence briefly falters, but the band plays on, oblivious.
